speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health beyond bed occupancy rates, ward admission waiting times and emergency department attendances, what additional public health indicators the Ministry will publish on a monthly or bi-weekly basis to enable the public to better track health outcomes and system pressures, in light of Singapore’s transition to a super-aged society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: For example, several capacity related indicators are available on the MOH website.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The National Nutritional Survey informs us of the dietary patterns and nutritional status of the population.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: In addition, indicators on cancer, chronic kidney failure, stroke and heart attack are also published by the National Registry of Disease Office annually.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My question really starts from the debate at the Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister of State referred to the Budget Book.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are two particular key performance indicators (KPIs) there, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One is "the percentage of patients who wait less than or 100 minutes for consultations at polyclinics".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is another one which says "the percentage of patients who waited more than or equal to 60 days for new subsidised specialist outpatient clinic appointments".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My question was framed with regard to our super-aged society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The consideration that I am suggesting that MOH looks into is whether there could be a public health dashboard for Singaporeans that gives us a one-stop identifiable datapoint on what our public healthcare outcomes are looking like on a bi-weekly or monthly basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, these two KPIs in the Budget Book, for example, could potentially be on that dashboard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are other Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries which also have public health dashboards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My query ultimately is, how is MOH going to look at improving reporting of these public health outcomes in the context of a super-aged society and not prior to this Rubicon that we have now crossed?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Perhaps I could just give some insight also as to how we have framed this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: When we look at how we are tracking and measuring, we look at an end-to-end and a full suite approach to things: we look at the preventive efforts that we are doing, and that is why we are tracking screening rates, enrolment to Healthier SG; we look at the aspect of the systems and the pressures on that; the access to care is also one dimension; we also look at the larger health outcomes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is actually a full range, and in that sense, many of these are already available, that datapoint is already available to the public to scrutinise and look at.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I take note of some of the items that the Member has raised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There needs to be a balance in what we are tracking, because just providing the information may not provide any meaningful insight or will necessarily encourage the right behaviours.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, when we look at Emergency Department timings, the point of it is really that at the end of the day for Emergency Departments, if it is an emergency case, it will be attended to immediately.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Regardless of the median waiting times or whatever, there is already a protocol that is in place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The point is, we also want to then nudge behaviours.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: That particular measure may not necessarily reflect the efforts we are taking in that space.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I will take the feedback back and we will continue to review this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister of State mentioned meaningful impact a few times, so I will give an example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The KPI in the Budget Book, "the percentage of patients who waited less than or at least 100 minutes for consultations at polyclinics", for example, for each fiscal year, 2023, 2024, 2025 – the number is 99%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, it is very high degree in terms of hitting the KPI.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But at some point we have to ask, is that a meaningful representation of what constitutes a good public health outcome?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is 100 minutes too lax or two permissive a KPI?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I think if you have a public health dashboard, for example, with a little bit more granularity, I believe the public would have a better sense of the stressors on the healthcare system and where improvements can be made, and where changes also can be advanced in Parliament and out of Parliament to achieve better outcomes for the population at large.
